"Terminus" means the end point of something — the very last point, the final stop, the furthest limit something reaches before it goes no further. Everything about this word points to finality.
The most everyday meaning: the last stop on a transport route

This is where most people encounter the word. When a train, bus, or subway line runs from one place to another, the final station at each end of that route is called a terminus. Once the train pulls in there, the journey is over. Everyone must get off — there is nowhere left to go on that particular line.

For example, if a train runs between two cities and stops at City B with no track continuing beyond it, City B is the terminus of that line. It's worth noting that a single route has two termini (that's the plural of terminus — more on plurals below) — one at each end. The word "terminus" on a sign at a station essentially means: "This is it. The line ends here."
The broader meaning: the end of anything

The word isn't locked to trains and buses. It can describe the final point of almost any physical thing that has length or extent.

The terminus of a glacier, for instance, is the lowest, furthest-forward point where the ice ends — where it stops advancing and starts melting. The terminus of a road or a path is simply the spot where it runs out and you can go no further in that direction. The terminus of a pipeline is the point where it delivers its contents and ends.

In a slightly more abstract sense, writers and thinkers sometimes use "terminus" to describe the final conclusion or outcome of something non-physical — the end point of a chain of events, a line of reasoning, or a long process. In this sense, the word carries a feeling of inevitability and finality: whatever journey was being made, this is where it was always heading.

In an older, more formal sense — one you're more likely to encounter in historical or legal writing than in everyday conversation — a terminus can refer to a physical stone, post, or marker placed in the ground to indicate the boundary between two pieces of land or two territories. It marked, in a concrete and permanent way, where one thing ended and another began. This sense is rare in modern everyday speech but still appears in texts dealing with land law, surveying, or history.
Two important academic phrases: terminus post quem and terminus ante quem

If you ever read books on history, archaeology, or literary scholarship, you'll likely come across two Latin phrases built around the word "terminus." They are extremely useful tools for dating things when you don't have an exact date, and understanding them will serve you well.

Terminus post quem (often shortened to TPQ) means the earliest possible point in time at which something could have been made, written, or happened. In other words, it's the "no earlier than" boundary. Imagine researchers discover an ancient manuscript that mentions a particular king who came to power in the year 1200. That means the manuscript couldn't have been written before 1200, because its author knew about that king. The year 1200 is therefore the terminus post quem of that manuscript — the limit after which it must have been created.

Terminus ante quem (often shortened to TAQ) works in the opposite direction. It means the latest possible point in time at which something could have been made or happened — the "no later than" boundary. Imagine archaeologists find a building that was destroyed by fire in 1350, and they discover objects buried in its floor. Those objects must have been placed there before 1350, when the building was still standing. The year 1350 is therefore the terminus ante quem — the limit before which those objects must have been buried.

Together, these two phrases allow scholars to pin something between two dates, creating a window of possibility even without a single confirmed date. They are precise, elegant tools for thinking about time.

"Terminus" has two accepted plural forms, and both are correct. "Termini" is the Latin-style plural and is considered more formal — you'll often see it in academic writing or in the context of transport networks. "Terminuses" is the standard English-style plural and is more common in everyday casual usage. You can use either without being wrong, though "termini" tends to sound more polished.
The single idea that unifies all the meanings

No matter which context you see "terminus" used in, the word always answers one question: Where does this end? It is always about a definitive stopping point — a place or moment where something reaches its limit and goes no further. Whether it's the last station on a railway line, the tip of a melting glacier, the edge of a territorial boundary, or the outer limit of a possible date range, "terminus" marks that final, clear edge where something stops being what it was and simply ends.
